chunks: "A PoP stack changes the thermal picture in two ways. The memory sits right on top of the SoC, which is the hottest part.

Normally an SoC can push a good chunk of its heat up through the top of its package into a heat spreader or the case; with PoP, that path goes through the memory package first, which is a stack of mould compound, substrate and DRAM silicon, so the top path has much higher thermal resistance.
Heat therefore goes mostly down through the solder balls into the board's copper, and some goes up through the memory.
The result is that the SoC runs hotter for the same power, and the DRAM is heated from underneath by the SoC.

DRAM is temperature-sensitive: above about 85 degrees C its cells leak faster, so the controller has to refresh more often, which costs power and bandwidth, and past its maximum rating it can't be used reliably.
I think of it as a thermal circuit. If the SoC has 32 K/W down through the board to ambient and 20 K/W up with no memory, those are in parallel, so about 12. 3 K/W.
Add the memory's 15 K/W in series with the top path and the up path becomes 35 K/W, so the total becomes about 16. 7 K/W, a 36% increase.
At 3 watts that's about 50 K rise instead of 37.
To manage it you improve the board path with copper and vias, put a thermal pad or graphite sheet over the memory to the case, and use the SoC's own thermal throttling.
Past a few watts of sustained power, PoP stops being practical, which is why it's a mobile technology and not used on high-power chips."
